offence_severity: Minimum sentence provided is seven years but it may extend to imprisonment for life
physical_harm: Severe burn injuries on approximately 55% of the body including head, face, neck, breast, left hand and right hand from front and back side
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC; finally upheld under Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the third dying declaration dated 13.02.2008, which stated that the appellant poured kerosene oil on the deceased and set her on fire, and found it reliable due to the deceased's specific and unambiguous statement without implicating others involved in the dowry harassment.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, noting that the first two dying declarations were recorded under circumstances that raised doubts about their voluntariness, while the third was considered reliable due to the deceased's specific and unambiguous statement and the presence of her parents during its recording.
trial_duration: Offence: 02.02.2008; Trial judgment: 25.03.2010; High Court decision: 29.06.2017; Supreme Court decision: 28.01.2020
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Aakash Sirohi, Indra Lal, M. P. Shorawala; Counsel for the State: Dr. Rajiv Nanda, Manish Kumar Vikkey
investigation_status: FIR registered on 29.02.2008; charge sheet filed under Sections 304-B and 498-A of IPC
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Convicted under Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, affirmed conviction, modified sentence
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased was subjected to cruelty and harassment by her in-laws for dowry, leading to her unnatural death within seven years of marriage, thereby invoking the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act that the appellant caused the dowry death. They also emphasized the reliability of the third dying declaration and the failure of the accused to rebut the presumption.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to present material to rule out accidental death, establish ongoing dowry harassment, and that the parents of the deceased did not report the dowry demand. They also contended that the High Court erred in relying on the dying declarations without proper corroboration and in reversing the trial court's acquittal.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that once the prosecution establishes the ingredients of Section 304-B IPC, the accused must rebut the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act. It also considered the reliability of dying declarations and the necessity of corroboration.
precedent_relied_upon: Nallam Veera Stayanandam & Ors. v. The Public Prosecutor, High Court of A.P. (2004) 10 SCC 769; Ashabai & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra (2013) 2 SCC 224; State of Karnataka v. Suvarnamma & Anr. (2015) 1 SCC 323; Hem Chand v. State of Haryana (1994) 6 SCC 727
sentencing_rationale: The sentence of life imprisonment was altered to rigorous imprisonment for seven years, including the period already served, due to mitigating factors such as the appellant's age, her contribution to the family, and the husband's age, in line with the principle that extreme punishment under Section 304-B should be rare.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The appellant's age, her contribution to the family, and the husband's age were considered as mitigating factors.
other_sentence_order: Fine as imposed and default sentence is sustained.
